title: The Return of the Wolves
intro: Wolves disappeared from Yellowstone National Park in the 1920s. Their return in the 1990s became one of the most famous experiments in ecology – but the story may be more complicated than it first seemed.

passage: For much of the twentieth century, there were no wolves in Yellowstone, the oldest national park in the United States. Wolves had been hunted, trapped and poisoned across the western states because farmers saw them as a threat to their cattle and sheep, and by the 1920s the last wolves in the park had been killed. At the time, few people thought this was a loss. Wolves were regarded as dangerous pests, and removing them was considered part of making the land safe and productive.

Over the following decades, however, scientists began to notice changes. Without a major predator, the number of elk – large deer that feed on grass, young trees and bushes – grew rapidly. Elk spent long periods beside rivers and streams, where they ate young willow and aspen trees before they could grow tall. As these trees disappeared, the riverbanks became less stable, and animals that depended on them, such as songbirds and beavers, became harder to find. Some ecologists began to argue that the park was out of balance and that the missing piece was the wolf.

The idea of bringing wolves back was extremely controversial. Ranchers living near the park feared that wolves would leave the protected area and attack their livestock, while hunters worried about competition for elk. After years of public debate, the plan finally went ahead. In 1995 and 1996, a little over thirty grey wolves were captured in Canada, transported to Yellowstone and kept in large fenced areas for several weeks so that they could get used to their new home before being released. Each animal was fitted with a radio collar so that scientists could follow its movements.

The wolves adapted remarkably quickly. They formed packs, raised pups and began hunting elk, and their numbers rose steadily over the following decade, until there were more than a hundred wolves living in several packs. Researchers who followed the animals noticed that the elk were changing their behaviour too. Instead of standing for hours in open valleys and along rivers, they moved more often and avoided places where they could easily be trapped. Some scientists described this as a 'landscape of fear'.

What happened next has become one of the most famous stories in ecology. In some areas, willows and aspens began to grow back, and with more trees along the rivers, beavers returned and built dams that created new wetlands for fish, frogs and birds. This chain of effects, in which a predator at the top of the food chain influences plants and animals far below it, is known as a trophic cascade. Some researchers have even suggested that bears benefited, because more berry bushes grew in places where elk no longer fed. Videos telling this story online have been watched millions of times.

However, many researchers now believe that the popular version is too simple. They point out that elk numbers also fell because of drought, hunting outside the park and an increase in other predators, including bears and cougars. Studies of trees have produced mixed results: in some places willows clearly recovered, but in others they are still struggling. As one scientist put it, wolves are important, but they are not a magic switch that can repair a damaged ecosystem by themselves.

Whatever the scientific debate, the wolves have brought one undeniable benefit. Wolf-watching has become a popular activity, particularly in the Lamar Valley, and visitors who come hoping to see the animals spend money in local hotels, restaurants and shops. Conflict with ranchers has not disappeared, and wolves that leave the park can still be legally hunted in some neighbouring states. Yet the Yellowstone experiment has changed the way many people think about predators – not as enemies to be removed, but as part of a living system that is still not fully understood.
